sections.h2: What should a seller understand about New Jersey before opening a city or county guide?
sections.html:
New Jersey is small, crowded and divided into many local governments, so the rules that touch a sale change more by town and county than by state. Wikipedia lists it as the fifth-smallest state by land area at 7,354 square miles, with 21 counties and 564 municipalities, and every New Jersey county counts as urban for Census Bureau purposes. Because all land sits inside a municipality, almost every seller deals with a town-level tax office, a town-level construction office and a county-level clerk.

The July 2025 Census estimate counts 9,548,215 residents, compared with 9,288,994 in the 2020 count. That spread of people over a small area is why a seller in a dense Hudson County town and one in a Sussex County borough can face very different buyer pools, even though the same state forms apply to both.

Start with the guide for the town and county of your house, then use the topics below for rules that apply everywhere in the state.

sections.h2: How expensive and owner-heavy is housing across New Jersey?
sections.html:
QuickFacts gives a statewide look at ownership and cost, and local values can sit far above or below it.

Roughly one resident in five and a half is 65 or older, the group that senior-focused tax programs target.

sections.h2: Which New Jersey counties hold the most people, and how do regions differ?
sections.html:
The six largest counties by the 2020 census, according to Wikipedia's county table, are Bergen with 955,732 residents, Essex with 863,728, Middlesex with 863,162, Hudson with 724,854, Monmouth with 643,615 and Ocean with 637,229. At the other end, Salem County had 64,837.

The state's geography shapes what a seller sees.

  • Northeast and the Gateway Region: closest to Manhattan, with up to a million residents commuting daily, according to Wikipedia.
  • Skylands: the wooded, rural and mountainous northwest, where High Point in Sussex County is the highest elevation at 1,803 feet.
  • Pine Barrens: the pine and oak forest of the southern interior, with a lower population density than most of the state.
  • Jersey Shore: a coastline reached by the Garden State Parkway, with homes exposed to nor'easters and occasional tropical storms, including the 2012 hurricane landfall.

The state is broadly divided into North, Central and South Jersey, though some residents do not treat Central Jersey as a region of its own.

sections.h2: How do property tax appeals and relief programs work across the state?
sections.html:
Assessment challenges start at the county board of taxation. The Division of Taxation sets April 1 as the usual filing cutoff, moved to May 1 in towns that just finished a revaluation or reassessment.

Three counties break the pattern: Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth use a January 15 cutoff. An assessment above $1,000,000 opens a shortcut to the state Tax Court, and anyone unhappy with a board ruling has 45 days to go there.

Relief for owners comes from two levels. The state pays Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ, while each town applies its own deductions for seniors, disabled persons and veterans. The 2025 application period ended November 2, 2026. Ask your county board for its local office numbers, since they differ across the 21 counties.

sections.h2: What does a New Jersey seller pay at closing?
sections.html:
Under the Division of Taxation's home sale guide, no sales tax applies and the seller carries a 1 percent Realty Transfer Fee. A buyer owes a further 1 percent only when the price reaches $1 million. The fee page expresses the base rate as dollars per $500 of price and adds a Graduated Percent Fee for residential deeds above $1,000,000.

  • Paperwork at recording: a GIT/REP form goes in with every deed.
  • In-state sellers: sign GIT/REP-3, then report any gain on the NJ-1040 the next spring.
  • Sellers who live elsewhere: prepay 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of net gain, unless an exemption on the form fits.
  • Gain on a main home: $250,000 can be excluded for one filer and $500,000 for a married couple filing together, after two years of owning and living there.

Gifts between spouses or from parent to child, and estate distributions to heirs, are among the deeds the fee page exempts.

sections.h2: How does a lender foreclose on a house in New Jersey?
sections.html:
New Jersey requires a lender to sue in court before the house can be sold off. NJ Courts says the lender begins with a written Notice of Intent, and the debtor has 30 days from receipt to pay or arrange something else. The complaint follows, and a defendant who wants to contest has 35 days to answer.

After default and final judgment, the court issues a writ of execution and the county sheriff has 150 days to auction the property. Debtor and lender may each request stays, and after the sale the debtor has 10 days to redeem. Free foreclosure mediation exists, and the court cautions against loan modification and rescue scams.

A homeowner who sells before the sheriff's sale avoids the auction. Court filing fees listed by NJ Courts are $405 for a complaint, $175 for an answer and $50 for a motion.

sections.h2: How do rental and eviction rules affect a sale?
sections.html:
Selling a rented house means the tenancy goes along with it. The statewide Anti-Eviction Act, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 and following, requires good cause to remove a residential tenant, and cases are heard in the Special Civil Part of Superior Court.

Only a Special Civil Part officer may carry out an eviction. The court's published filing cost is $50 for one defendant, and the trial date is at least 21 days after service. Foreclosure does not by itself force out a tenant with a valid lease.

The separate notice-length rules, the court steps and the tenant defenses each have their own statewide guide, each worth reading before a landlord-seller picks a closing date.

sections.h2: Where do local rules change from town to town?
sections.html:
Rent control is the clearest example. The Department of Community Affairs says New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but a municipality may adopt an ordinance, and the local rent control board or municipal clerk can say whether a unit is covered.

Property tax relief that depends on a municipality, such as the senior and veteran deductions, is filed with the local assessor or collector. Offices run by each county, such as the clerk and the tax board, vary in forms, fees and hours, so the county guides cover those.

Request the latest tax bill from the municipal tax collector and the construction or code office for any open permits before listing. Those two requests catch most surprises that slow a closing.

faqs.q: How many counties and municipalities does New Jersey have?
faqs.a: New Jersey has 21 counties and 564 municipalities, according to Wikipedia. All land in the state belongs to a municipality, so every property has both a town tax office and a county clerk.

faqs.q: What does the typical owner-occupied New Jersey home cost?
faqs.a: QuickFacts shows $454,400 as the midpoint for owner-occupied homes in 2020-2024. Local medians differ from town to town, so use that figure only as a statewide benchmark.

faqs.q: When must a New Jersey assessment appeal be filed?
faqs.a: April 1 in most places, according to the Division of Taxation, and May 1 after a town revaluation. Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth Counties instead use January 15.

faqs.q: Which side pays the state transfer fee when a New Jersey house sells?
faqs.a: The seller, at closing. The Division's guide puts the seller's share at 1 percent, with an added 1 percent on the buyer for prices at $1 million and up.

faqs.q: Is foreclosure handled by the court in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Yes. Yes. A lender must sue in court, and the county sheriff then runs the auction after a final judgment and a writ of execution.
